title: Taking a Look at Paperbag Dungeon - Dungeon-themed, tile-laying, puzzle card game
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nZ-Yf21ufww

Daniel (@dungeondive) looks at Dustin Porta's *Paperbag Dungeon*, a 2021 Solitaire Print-and-Play Contest winner for best new artist, now on The Game Crafter with a crowd sale coming. You are the palace's newly promoted head janitor, laying tunnel cards into a sprawling dungeon while keeping the monsters from crashing the royal wedding. Win by placing the whole deck or building a "perfect dungeon" with every passage sealed; lose if a monster forces your gate and escapes.

The hook is that the art is the rules. Skulls mark dead monsters that flip to live ones, hatches connect to every other hatch, gems are a currency spent by flipping their card, goblins trigger every other goblin in the dungeon, purple-shaded trip wires show a sprung trap, musical notes wake sleeping giants, and spiders drawn slipping through a grate tell you spiders pass grates. Daniel calls it a Where's Waldo of iconography, charming to pore over, though sometimes inconsistent or hidden under detail, and the five rule cards are too small to do the examples justice (Dustin's own rules video helped).

Play escalates through Chill, Janitor and Warden modes, adding vault cards, traps, hatches and monster placement rules: face-up monsters go as far from the gate as possible, skull-side ones as close as possible. Daniel calls it a mellow puzzle activity more than a game, unlike anything else in his collection, pleasing to look at when finished, and a good fit for tile-layers who want dungeon theme without combat.

----

When the artwork *is* the iconography, is a little ambiguity a fair price for cards this pretty, or should rules always be unmistakable?
